# PART FOUR OF THE FIRST BOOK

requires a moderation of the fire, and a gradual succession of its increase, with caution, until it is fixed in its own lime <note>the metallic oxide</note>, so that it does not easily return into a body <note>revert to a solid metallic state</note>, so that a greater fire can be administered to it for the perfection of its lime. Similarly, let him not happen to err in <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss> because of its difficult reduction; for if he should at any time put its lime to reduction, it may happen that it does not reduce, but he finds it in its prior state or turned into glass, and he might estimate its reduction to be impossible. For we say that if one does not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If indeed a great fire is used, it does not necessarily happen that it reduces, but it is possible to reduce it into vitrification <gloss>turning into glass</gloss>. And this is because <term>Jupiter</term> <margin>am ta</margin> <margin>cc</margin> has a fugitive substance of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> enclosed in the depth of its nature. If this substance endures a long delay in the fire, it will flee, and leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found to be converted more readily to vitrification than to the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own proper humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. Therefore it is necessarily left that one must hasten to reduce it quickly with a most swift impetus of fire. For otherwise it is not reduced. Therefore, let the craftsman be exercised in this, and he shall know. <margin>et</margin>

The second mode of calcination for these two bodies <gloss>Saturn and Jupiter</gloss> <margin>85, 6</margin> <note>Lead and Tin</note>, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown upon their surface, quantity after quantity very often during its fusion, and they should be mixed with much agitation by an iron rod over the fire until, through the mixing of salt, they are turned into ash. And afterwards, the lime of these should be perfected by the same mode of perfection, with its considerations. <margin>wooden. boiling. page 57, 14.</margin> But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>lead</term> <note>original: plumbum</note> is converted to powder from the first labors of calcination more easily than <term>Jupiter</term>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>Lead</gloss> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.

<summary>This page explains the technical difficulties of reducing tin from its lime, warning that excessive or prolonged heat can turn it into glass by driving off its internal mercury. It also describes a second method of calcination using salt and constant agitation to produce metallic ashes.</summary>
